notes.b: A household chooses a home by weighing what it needs and can afford against what is available in the place it wants to live.
points: Socio-economic factors include income, employment, household size and the stage of the family life cycle, such as young children, teenagers or an older couple whose children have left home.
Cost decides the size, type and location of home a household can afford; the deposit and running costs matter as much as the purchase price or rent.
Location is shaped by proximity to work, schools, shops, childcare, public transport, health services and family or friends.
Personal preference covers layout, aspect, view, garden size and whether the household wants to own or rent.
Special needs, such as those of older people or people with a disability, may call for single-storey living, step-free access or a stairlift.
Availability, meaning the supply of suitable homes at a given time and place, limits choice; in some urban areas private supply is short and social housing waiting lists are long.
Setting: a case study of a student, a young couple or a retired couple, asking which of these factors matters most to them.
Mixed house types are planned together in new estates, combining detached, semi-detached, terraced and apartment units.
New developments include shared open space, play areas and local shops, and some estates are gated.
Refurbishment and inner-city redevelopment bring vacant or derelict buildings back into residential use.
Apartment living and higher-density development grow in cities, using less land per household.
Eco-houses, built to high energy efficiency standards with renewable heating, are an emerging development trend.
Demand for housing in a particular area is driven by employment growth, which pulls people towards commuter towns and cities.

notes.b: The current national plan is Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025 to 2030. It sets the government's direction for housing supply, sustainability and support for households.
points: Sustainable communities: new housing should be supported by shops, schools, transport, parks and other infrastructure.
Social and affordable housing is a core element, delivered by local authorities, approved housing bodies and voluntary and co-operative housing organisations.
Energy-efficient homes are promoted through building standards, BER ratings and grants for upgrading existing homes.
Protection of listed buildings and the natural environment, with grants available to help retain listed buildings.
Supports to alleviate homelessness, and specific accommodation for Travellers.
Rent supports for tenants, and registration of rented accommodation so that rented homes are on a register.
Higher-density living and increased housing supply in urban areas, with the aim of making more homes available at affordable cost.

notes.h: Buying a home: advantages and disadvantages
points: Advantage: a home may rise in value, so it can act as an investment.
Advantage: security of tenure, because an owner cannot be asked to leave by a landlord.
Advantage: freedom to choose the design and type of home, to alter it, and to decide whether to share it with others.
Advantage: mortgage repayments may cost less than rent over the long term, and grants may apply to some purchases.
Disadvantage: a large deposit and a long financial commitment are needed before the purchase can be completed.
Disadvantage: legal, lending, survey and stamp duty fees add to the initial cost.
Disadvantage: the owner pays for all maintenance and repairs, including property tax where it applies.
Disadvantage: the value may fall, leaving the owner owing more than the home is worth.
Disadvantage: buying ties the household to one location, so moving is slow and expensive.

notes.h: Renting a home: advantages and disadvantages
points: Advantage: little capital is needed, usually only a deposit and rent paid in advance.
Advantage: mobility, so a household can move when work or family circumstances change.
Advantage: the landlord is normally responsible for structural repairs and maintenance.
Advantage: a wider choice of accommodation, from apartments and houses to shared houses and digs.
Advantage: tenants have legal protections, including notice periods before a tenancy can be ended.
Disadvantage: rent paid gives no return, often described as dead money.
Disadvantage: agency fees, a deposit and rent in advance add to the initial cost.
Disadvantage: the tenant must insure the contents of the home.
Disadvantage: facilities may be poor or shared, and the tenant has no say over changes to the property.
Private rented housing is provided by individual landlords and businesses; rent depends on demand and supply, location, size, quality and amenities.
Minimum physical standards apply: the property must be structurally sound, with safe gas and electricity supplies and good repair.
Every room must have adequate ventilation and lighting, and hot and cold water must be provided.
Bathrooms and showers must be in good working order and kept in a proper state of repair.
Landlords must register rented accommodation, which helps the state track rented housing and its standards.
Private renting is popular with students, young workers and people who are saving for a deposit to buy a home.

keyTerms.definition: Influences on housing choice that relate to a household's income, employment, size and stage of family life.
The supply of suitable homes at a given time and place, which limits what a household can choose.
The right to remain in a home without being asked to leave, enjoyed by an owner-occupier and protected for tenants by law.
Rent paid to a landlord that gives the tenant no return or ownership of the property.
A housing development supported by shops, schools, transport, amenities and infrastructure that allow residents to live and work locally.
Housing built at a greater number of homes per hectare, typically through apartments and terraced houses in urban areas.
Homes let by private landlords and businesses to tenants at market rents.
A home designed to high energy efficiency standards, often with renewable energy and sustainable materials.

factCards.term: Three factors that influence housing choice
factCards.definition: Cost, location and the size of the household. Personal preference and availability are also important.

factCards.term: Four features of national housing policy
factCards.definition: Sustainable communities with amenities; social and affordable housing; energy-efficient homes; supports to alleviate homelessness.

factCards.term: Three advantages of buying a home
factCards.definition: The home may rise in value as an investment; the owner has security of tenure; the owner can design, alter and choose how to use the home.

factCards.term: Three disadvantages of renting a home
factCards.definition: Rent gives no return; agency fees, deposit and advance rent add to costs; the tenant must insure the contents.

factCards.term: Groups that rely on local schools, shops and transport
factCards.definition: Families with children, who need schools and childcare; older people, who need shops and health services; commuters, who need public transport.

factCards.term: Why a landlord must maintain a rented home
factCards.definition: Minimum physical standards for rented accommodation require structural soundness, safe services and adequate ventilation, lighting and water.

questions.prompt: State two advantages and two disadvantages of a family renting a home.
questions.model: Advantages: little capital is needed, only a deposit and rent in advance; mobility to move when circumstances change; the landlord is normally responsible for structural repairs and maintenance; a wider choice of accommodation. Disadvantages: rent gives no return; agency fees, deposit and advance rent add to costs; the tenant must insure the contents; facilities may be poor or shared.

questions.prompt: Discuss the factors that influence a household's choice of housing, and comment on how national housing policy aims to meet the housing needs of households.
questions.model: Socio-economic factors: income and employment affect what can be afforded; household size and the stage of the family life cycle determine the number of rooms needed; children's schooling and older people's needs affect the choice. Cost: purchase price, deposit and running costs decide the size, type and location of home. Location: proximity to work, schools, shops, childcare, transport and family. Personal preference: layout, aspect, garden, and whether to own or rent. Special needs: single-storey living or step-free access for people with a disability or older people. Availability: the supply of suitable homes in the area, with long waiting lists for social housing in some places. Policy: sustainable communities supported by amenities and infrastructure; social and affordable housing provided by local authorities, approved housing bodies and co-operatives; energy-efficient homes; rent supports and registration of rented accommodation; supports for people experiencing homelessness; higher-density living in urban areas to increase supply.
